## Reviewer #1
## (Remarks to the Author)

I appreciate the care taken in revising the manuscript and thank the authors for their detailed responses. I think this paper is a significant contribution for understanding the genetic ancestry of the Biobank Japan cohort and links these insights in a very interesting and innovative way to phenotypic variation.
- The description of ancestry modelling using a previously proposed tripartite ancestry model is now much clearer.

- The authors have incorporated new analysis to address my concerns about residual confounding driving their signal of Jomon ancestry being associated with BMI. Following careful analysis, it appears as though the association has reduced by quite a bit and is now only marginally significant, which is a bit concerning. As now discussed by the authors in the main text, Jomon ancestry is acting as a weak confounder on the GWAS and inflates the PGS. How can we be sure that all confounding has now been removed? E.g. it could be that your inferred Jomon proportions are a bit noisy and so there is still some leftover confounding.

- You mention that the top hits for BMI are unchanged even when correcting for Jomon ancestry. This is certainly reassuring and suggests that if you compute the PGS with more stringent p-value cutoff than this should already reduce association in your original analysis as well. Could you check this?
- l. 312: Please report the updated beta and p-value of association after correcting for Jomon ancestry.

- It is interesting that 13% of the variance in Jomon ancestry is explained by the Jomon variants that were identified. I agree with the authors that this is a notable proportion and appreciate the added analyses to emphasise this.

- It does pose the question of why this is the case. As in my original review, I think the current manuscript is a bit weak in providing evolutionary interpretations on this phenomenon. Presumably this happens because there is strong drift in Jomon, and/or lots of unique mutations in Jomon that tag Jomon haplotypes. This must be unusual though, typically if ancestry is defined by small differences in allele frequency genome-wide than this type of approach should not work so well. Some simple summary statistics, such as the global frequencies of these Jomon variants, would be helpful in interpreting this phenomenon.
## Reviewer #2
## (Remarks to the Author)

Thank you for your sincere responses and additional analyses in addressing my comments and questions. The manuscript now presents a clearer message regarding the contribution of Jomon ancestry to a particular phenotype related to BMI. It is particularly noteworthy to detect extended haplotypes for Jomon-related variants, supporting the potential for positive selection.

1. Among the 132 independent Jomon-related variants, how many exhibit significantly longer haplotypes compared to nonJomon-related variants? Additionally, among these longer haplotypes, are any specifically associated with BMI? This examination is crucial for understanding the potential positive selection on this phenotype introduced by Jomon admixture into the contemporary Japanese population.

2. Without clear evidence, it is challenging to comprehend why only BMI is significantly associated with Jomon ancestry among other traits (as shown in Fig 4), considering that Jomon admixture would occur randomly across the genome. This point also pertains to the conclusion that increasing BMI in the Japanese population is introduced by Jomon ancestry.

3. In modern populations, a high BMI is generally considered a risk factor. While this knowledge can positively impact the interpretation of GWAS results, it may also lead to negative perceptions of Jomon admixture among the public. Therefore, it becomes important to reveal the evolutionary story of this trait's adaptation, not only for the Jomon but also for the Yayoi populations. Alternatively, the authors could describe the potential positive influences of high BMI in certain contexts.

By addressing these points, the manuscript will emphasize novel finding and provide a more comprehensive understanding of the evolutionary implications and public health perspectives of BMI-related Jomon ancestry in the contemporary Japanese population.

## Reviewer #1
## (Remarks to the Author)
Thank you for your responses and overall I am happy with all the revisions made and think this is an important contribution.

I very much appreciate all the robustness checks done for the association between Jomon ancestry and BMI. It is encouraging that the signal is robust to excluding people from Okinawa, and age/sex effects. Some association between PGS and Jomon ancestry remains after correcting for Jomon ancestry in the GWAS and so overall I would say I believe your result. But I am still confused by your interpretation of the result when correcting for Jomon proportions and perhaps you can include a clarifying sentence around the paragraph starting in line 311:

In my understanding, ideally you want the *true effect sizes* for BMI at every SNP, and then compute PGS and correlate to Jomon ancestry. Now we of course don't have true effect sizes and so have to estimate these using GWAS. You get very slightly different effect sizes depending on whether you incorporate Jomon ancestry as a covariate, and as you mention in the main text and your response you say
"Jomon ancestry acts as a confounding factor in estimating effect sizes for BMI".

In fact you say "Jomon ancestry works as a confounder in BMI GWAS, supporting the validity of the association between Jomon ancestry and BMI". That doesn't make sense to me, you could make the same argument for any of the covariates but it would usually be false? Or at least it wouldn't be a genetic association. Are you saying there are real interactions between global Jomon ancestry and the true effect size? I’m not sure that seems plausible.. More plausibly, the pre-Jomon corrected effect sizes are somewhat biased due to some residual confounding.
